state.misconception_label: Believes if you changed all values by the same proportion the range would not change

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are discussing the \( 5 \) plants with these heights: \( 24 \mathrm{~cm}, 17 \mathrm{~cm}, 42 \mathrm{~cm}, 26 \mathrm{~cm}, 13 \mathrm{~cm} \) Tom says if all the plants were cut in half, the range wouldn't change. Katie says if all the plants grew by \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) each, the range wouldn't change. Who do you agree with? I got Only
Tom because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Let's think about it this way: if you have a group of friends who are all different heights, and you cut each of them in half, do you think the range of their heights would stay the same? Or if they all grew by the same amount, would the range still be the same? Think about how changing all the values by the same proportion affects the spread of the data.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh right, so if everyone grows by 3 cm, the difference between the tallest and shortest person would still be the same because they both grew the same amount... but if we cut them all in half, wouldn't the range get smaller because all the numbers are smaller? So maybe Katie is right and Tom is wrong?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: That's a great observation! Just like how cutting your friends in half would change the range of their heights, cutting the plants in half would also change the range of their heights. So, Katie is correct in this situation. Keep thinking about how changes in values affect the spread of the data.

score.justification_pass1: The teacher effectively addresses the specific misconception about proportional changes, the student demonstrates clear reasoning improvement by correctly distinguishing between additive and multiplicative changes by Turn 2, and the mathematical content is accurate throughout.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently grounds the abstract mathematical concept of range in a concrete, relatable real-world analogy (friends' heights) and uses this everyday situation to help the student reason through how transformations affect data spread.
